unit.title: Perform weld in flat and horizontal positions using gas tungsten metal arc welding process (GTAW) - (Tungsten inert gas - TIG)

summary: This unit teaches you to weld thin carbon steel, stainless steel and aluminium with gas tungsten arc welding (GTAW), usually called TIG welding, in the flat and horizontal positions. You will learn to work safely with a strong ultraviolet arc, high-frequency starting, argon and tungsten dust; choose the current, polarity, tungsten, gas and filler rod; grind and fit the tungsten; make butt, lap and fillet welds with a steady torch and filler rod; and inspect your welds, put faults right and report problems.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 2 qualification (MEM22423). It teaches **gas tungsten arc welding (GTAW)**, known in the workshop as **TIG welding** (tungsten inert gas), in the **flat** and **horizontal** positions: setting up the machine, the gas and the tungsten, choosing the settings and filler rod, and making neat, sound welds on thin metal.

TIG gives the cleanest, most controlled welds of any hand process. In Jamaica it is used wherever the weld must look good and stay clean: stainless steel tables, sinks and hoods in hotel and restaurant kitchens, food and drink processing plants, pipework in factories and sugar and rum works, handrails and balustrades, aluminium boat fittings and truck boxes, and repairs to thin, delicate parts. It is slower than MIG, so it is chosen for quality rather than speed.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 2 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres. You will weld 1.5–3 mm carbon steel with ER70S-2 or ER70S-6 rod on direct current, and learn the differences for stainless steel and aluminium.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Control the hazards of UV light, electric shock, high-frequency starting, ozone and fume, argon, tungsten dust, solvents and hot metal; wear the right PPE.
Read the drawing and welding procedure for the metal, thickness, joint, position, current, tungsten, gas and filler rod.
Set up the machine and gas
Choose DCEN or AC, set the current, pre-flow and post-flow; fit the regulator/flowmeter, leak-test and set the argon flow.
Choose the tungsten type and size, grind it correctly, and fit it with the matching collet, collet body and cup at the right stick-out.
Clean the metal and rod, fit up thin sheet tightly, and tack it at short distances.
Weld in the flat and horizontal positions
Hold a short arc and the right torch and rod angles, dab the rod into the pool in a steady rhythm, and make butt, lap and fillet welds.
Check welds front and back and with a fillet gauge, name faults and their causes, shut down safely, and report problems.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on the process, shielding gas, current and polarity, tungstens, the torch, safety, fume, cleaning, filler rods, technique, defects and inspection.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact trade words such as collet, back cap, cup, pre-flow, 2F and 1G) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: grinding and fitting your own tungsten, then a butt weld (1G) and a lap weld in thin carbon steel sheet; and tee fillet welds in the horizontal position (2F) in 3 mm plate, checked with a fillet gauge and written up on an inspection sheet.

blocks.note: TIG rewards patience. Most faults come from three habits: a dirty joint, a long arc, and a tungsten that touches the pool or rod. Work on those first.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: In TIG welding, an arc burns between a **tungsten electrode** and the work. Tungsten melts at about 3 400 °C, far hotter than the arc needs to melt steel, so the electrode **does not melt** into the weld: it only carries the arc. The arc melts the edges of the joint into a small pool. When filler metal is needed, you feed a **filler rod** into the pool by hand, with your other hand. An **inert gas**, usually pure **argon**, flows out of the torch cup and protects the tungsten, the pool and the hot end of the rod from the air. There is no flux, no slag and almost no spatter.

head: Name
What it means
rows: Gas tungsten arc welding: the official name
A TIG weld made with no filler rod, just melting the edges together (used on some thin edge and corner joints)

head: Strengths
Limits
rows: Very fine control of heat: ideal for thin sheet
Clean, neat welds with no slag and little spatter
Welds carbon steel, stainless steel, aluminium, copper and more
Heat and filler are controlled separately
Needs very clean metal: there is no flux
Needs two steady hands, and often a foot
Wind easily blows the argon away

head: Code
Also called
What it is
rows: Butt (groove) weld in the flat position: plates flat, welded from above
Butt weld in the horizontal position: plates upright, the joint running across
Fillet weld in the flat position: the joint tilted so the weld lies in a trough
Fillet weld in the horizontal position: for example a tee joint with the base plate flat on the bench

blocks.note: In the codes, **G** means a groove (butt) weld and **F** a fillet weld; **1** is flat and **2** is horizontal. A lap joint laid flat on the bench is strictly a horizontal fillet, though job sheets often call it flat.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: TIG makes little smoke and almost no spatter, so it can look safe. It is not. The arc gives off **very strong ultraviolet (UV) and infrared light**, stronger than many other processes because there is no smoke to dim it, and stronger still with argon and on shiny aluminium and stainless steel.

head: Hazard
What can happen
How you control it
rows: Arc eye, and burns to bare skin like severe sunburn within minutes; long exposure damages the skin. Reflections from shiny metal and pale walls burn too.
Helmet with a suitable shade, often about 10 to 12
Neck, wrists and arms fully covered
The torch and leads carry welding current; sweat and wet surfaces let current through the skin.
The HF spark used to start the arc can upset heart pacemakers and other implants, and nearby computers, phones and electronic controls.
Anyone with a pacemaker or implant takes medical advice first
Follow the maker's instructions; use lift-arc where possible
UV light turns oxygen in the air into **ozone**, which irritates the eyes, nose and lungs; there is more on aluminium and with argon. Coatings and stainless steel give harmful fume.
Heavier than air, with no smell: it collects in pits, tanks and low spaces and pushes out the oxygen. A person can collapse without warning.
Cylinder closed when not in use
No welding in closed spaces without proper controls
Thoriated tungsten is slightly radioactive. Grinding makes a dust that is harmful if breathed in.
A grinder kept for tungsten only, with extraction
Or use lanthanated or ceriated tungsten instead
Acetone catches fire easily. **Chlorinated** degreasers near the arc are turned by its UV into **phosgene**, a poisonous gas.
A little acetone on a rag, allowed to dry, kept away from the arc
No chlorinated solvents anywhere near welding
Thin work and the rod end get hot very fast; the tungsten stays hot after welding.
Pliers for hot work; hot work marked

head: PPE
What it protects you from
Points to check
rows: Welding helmet, filter often about shade 10 to 12
UV and infrared on the eyes and face
Shade suits the current: darker for more amps
Auto-darkening helmet checked: TIG at low current can fail to trigger a weak sensor
Grinding the tungsten, wire brushing and cleaning; worn under the helmet
Heat and UV, while giving the fine feel needed for the torch and rod
Dry, no holes; heavier gloves for grinding and handling plate
Flame-resistant long-sleeved jacket, buttoned at the neck
UV burns on the arms, chest and neck

blocks.note: Because TIG is quiet and clean, welders are tempted to roll up their sleeves in Jamaica's heat. The UV from a TIG arc burns a bare forearm faster than the midday sun. Cover up, drink water and take short breaks instead.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: The TIG set: current, polarity and torch

blocks.p: A TIG machine is a **constant current (CC)** power source: the current stays close to what you set even when the arc length changes a little. You set the current on the machine, and on most machines you control it while welding with a **foot pedal** or a control on the torch. Many machines also let you set the **pre-flow**, **post-flow**, **up-slope** (the current rising gently at the start) and **down-slope** (the current falling gently at the end).

head: Current
How it is connected
Where the heat goes
Used for
rows: Torch to the negative (−) terminal; work lead to the positive (+)
About two-thirds into the work, one-third into the tungsten
Carbon steel, stainless steel, copper: deep, narrow penetration, and the tungsten stays cool and keeps its point
The current swaps direction many times a second
Shared between the work and the tungsten
Aluminium and magnesium: each electrode-positive half of the cycle breaks up the oxide skin (the cleaning action); each electrode-negative half heats the work
Hardly ever used for TIG: the tungsten overheats and melts unless it is very thick

blocks.note: Check the polarity before every job. On a DC-only machine, a torch plugged into the positive socket will melt the end off the tungsten in seconds.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Method
How it works
Points to know
rows: A high-voltage, high-frequency spark jumps from the tungsten to the work and starts the arc without touching
Clean starts; the spark can upset electronics and implants
Touch the tungsten lightly on the work, press the switch, and lift: the machine starts the arc at a low current, then rises to the set current
No HF; the tungsten barely touches, so contamination is small
Strike the tungsten on the work like a match
Used only on simple machines; it contaminates the tungsten and can leave tungsten in the weld

head: Part
Its job
Check
rows: A split sleeve that **grips the tungsten**
Holds the collet and passes the gas through holes to the cup
Same size as the tungsten; screwed in tight
Gas lens (in place of a collet body)
Fine mesh screens that make the gas flow out smooth and even, so the tungsten can stick out further and still be covered
A ceramic cup that directs the gas over the tungsten and the pool
No cracks or chips; size suits the job (cups are numbered in sixteenths of an inch: a No. 6 is about 9.5 mm across inside, a No. 8 about 12.7 mm)
Screws onto the back of the torch, covers the end of the tungsten and tightens the collet
Long or short to suit the tungsten and the space; O-ring sound
Starts the gas and the arc; the pedal also changes the current while you weld
Carries the current and the gas (and cooling water on a water-cooled torch)

blocks.p: Most training torches are **air-cooled** and suit lower currents. Higher currents need a **water-cooled** torch, with a cooling unit that must be running and full before you weld.

With a standard collet body, the tungsten usually sticks out about **3–6 mm** past the cup. A gas lens allows more, often about 10 mm, which helps to reach into the root of a fillet weld while keeping good gas cover.

Pure tungsten has small amounts of other oxides added to make the arc start more easily and stay steady. The type is shown by a **coloured band** on one end. Colours differ slightly between the European (ISO) and American (AWS) systems, so read the box too.

head: Type
Colour band
Typical use
rows: AC on aluminium with older transformer machines; forms a ball on the end
DC on steel and stainless; very good arc, but slightly radioactive
DC and AC; a common safer choice in place of thoriated
DC and AC, especially at low currents
AC on aluminium; holds a ball end well

blocks.note: Many centres now prefer **lanthanated** or **ceriated** tungstens to thoriated ones, because they work well on both DC and AC and are not radioactive. If thoriated tungsten is used, grind it only on the grinder kept for it, with the extraction on.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: The tungsten diameter must suit the current. Too small, and the tip overheats, melts into a ball or drops into the weld. Too big for a low current, and the arc is unsteady and wanders.

blocks.note: These are guide figures for pointed tungstens on DCEN; AC ranges are lower. Use the welding procedure and the tungsten maker's chart. For the thin carbon steel in this unit, 1.6 mm or 2.4 mm tungsten is usual.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Grinding a point for DC welding

flow: Put on safety glasses and switch on the extraction
Use only the grinder kept for tungsten (often a fine diamond wheel), so the tungsten picks up no steel or dirt
Hold the tungsten so that it points the way the wheel turns and the **grinding marks run along its length** towards the tip, never round it
Grind a taper about **2 to 2.5 times the tungsten's diameter** long (about 4–6 mm on a 2.4 mm tungsten)
Leave a very small flat on the very tip, so it does not burn away or break off into the weld
Check that the point is central and the taper even all round

blocks.p: Marks along the length let the arc leave the tip in a straight, steady column. Marks round the tungsten make the arc jump about and wander. A very short, blunt taper gives a wider arc and a wider, shallower weld; a very long, needle-sharp point is fragile and can break off.

On older transformer machines, a **pure** or **zirconiated** tungsten is used on AC, and its end forms a small, smooth **ball** as it heats. Modern inverter machines often use a lanthanated or ceriated tungsten ground to a slightly blunt point, even on AC. Follow the procedure and your instructor.

flow: Choose the type and size from the procedure
Fit a collet and collet body (or gas lens) of the **same size** as the tungsten
Slide the tungsten in and set the stick-out (about 3–6 mm with a standard collet body)
Screw the back cap on by hand to grip it
Fit a cup to suit the job, and check nothing is cracked or loose

blocks.p: If the tungsten touches the pool or the filler rod, metal sticks to it and the arc becomes wide, wandering and dirty. **Stop**, take the tungsten out, break or grind off the contaminated end, and re-point it on the tungsten grinder. Carrying on spreads tungsten and dirt into the weld.

The shielding gas keeps the air away from the **hot tungsten**, the **weld pool** and the **hot end of the filler rod**. Without it, oxygen burns the tungsten, and oxygen and nitrogen make the weld porous and oxidised.

ul: Use **pure argon** for carbon steel, stainless steel and aluminium. Some jobs use argon and helium mixes for more heat; your procedure will say.
**Never** use carbon dioxide, or the argon/CO2 mixes made for MIG welding: they attack the hot tungsten and spoil the weld. Check the cylinder label every time.
A typical flow with a standard cup, indoors, is about **7–12 litres per minute**. Larger cups and gas lenses need a little more. Too much flow becomes turbulent and pulls air in.
Set **pre-flow** so gas clears the air from the torch before the arc starts.

Set **post-flow** so gas keeps covering the tungsten and the crater while they cool. A common rule of thumb is about 1 second for every 10 A, with a few seconds as the least. Hold the torch still over the end of the weld until the gas stops.
Screen the work from fans, open doors and the wind.

flow: Check that the label says argon (or the mix the procedure gives), and chain the cylinder upright
Check the valve outlet and regulator threads are clean, undamaged and free of oil
Fit the argon regulator/flowmeter and tighten it with the correct spanner
Stand to one side and open the cylinder valve slowly
Leak-test the joints with leak-detection fluid
Press the torch switch or gas test button and set the flow; set the pre-flow and post-flow on the machine

blocks.h: Reading the colour of the tungsten

head: Tungsten after welding
What it tells you
rows: Good gas cover and enough post-flow
Post-flow too short, or the torch moved away too soon
Grey or black, perhaps with a crusty coating
Little or no gas: empty cylinder, closed valve, leak, draught or wrong gas

blocks.p: On a full-penetration weld in stainless steel, the **back** of the weld is also hot enough to react with the air. Without protection it turns grey and crusty, called **sugaring**: badly oxidised metal that will corrode. The cure is a **back purge**: argon is fed to the back of the joint (inside a pipe, or under a strip of tape or a purge box) to push the air out before and during welding.

blocks.note: Argon is heavier than air. It pools in pits, tanks, pipes and low corners, and you cannot see or smell it. Close the cylinder valve when you stop, and never enter or weld inside a purged pipe or tank.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Preparing the work and choosing filler rod

blocks.p: TIG has **no flux**, so nothing cleans the metal for you. Oil, grease, paint, rust, moisture, fingerprints and dust go straight into the weld as **porosity**, **poor fusion**, **cracks** and a dirty finish, and they contaminate the tungsten.

ul: Clean the joint and about 25 mm each side to **bright metal** with a grinder, file or wire brush.

Keep separate stainless steel brushes for **stainless steel** and for **aluminium**, and use them on nothing else. A brush used on mild steel leaves steel particles that rust on stainless and contaminate aluminium.
Wipe the joint with a clean, lint-free rag and a little **acetone**; let it dry fully before you strike. Keep the solvent and rags away from the arc.
Never use chlorinated solvents near welding.
Keep filler rods in their packet or a labelled tube, wipe them before use, and handle them with clean gloves.
Clean aluminium just before you weld: a new oxide skin starts forming straight away.

blocks.note: Jamaica's humid, salty air near the coast puts a film of moisture and salt on metal overnight. Clean and wipe the joint just before you weld, not the day before.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Metal
Usual filler rod
Points to know
rows: ER = electrode or rod; 70 = 70 000 psi minimum tensile strength; S = solid. The -2 rod has extra deoxidisers that suit TIG well.
The L means low carbon, which helps the weld resist corrosion. 316 stainless takes 316L.
4043 (aluminium-silicon) flows well and resists cracking; 5356 (aluminium-magnesium) is stronger

ul: Choose a rod diameter close to the metal thickness for thin work: about 1.6 mm rod for 1.5–2 mm sheet, about 2.4 mm rod for 3 mm.
TIG rods are about 1 m long and many are stamped with their grade. Stainless and steel rods look alike: keep them in labelled tubes and never mix them.
A rod of the wrong metal gives a weld that is weak, cracks or rusts.
Read the drawing for the sizes, joint and weld.
Thin sheet butt joints: fit the edges **tight together with no gap**, square and level. A gap in thin sheet melts away into a hole.
Tack at each end and then at **short distances** along the joint (often every 25–50 mm on 1.5–2 mm sheet), with small, well-fused tacks. Thin sheet moves as soon as it gets hot.
Tee joints: tack the upright square on the base at each end (and the middle on longer joints), and check with a square.
Clamp the work down, or to a heavy bar, to control distortion. Some jobs use a **copper backing bar** under a thin joint to draw heat away and support the penetration.

blocks.p: Thin sheet buckles easily, and **stainless steel buckles more than mild steel**: it expands more when hot and carries heat away more slowly, so the heat stays in one place. Keep the heat low, tack closely, clamp the work, and spread short welds along the job instead of finishing one long run.

sections.title: Welding technique in the flat and horizontal positions

blocks.p: Take the current from the welding procedure. If there is none, a rough starting point for **carbon steel** is about **30–40 A for each millimetre of thickness** (so roughly 60–80 A for 2 mm sheet), then test on scrap and adjust. Stainless steel usually needs a little less. With a foot pedal, set the machine a little above what you need and use the pedal to control it.

head: Setting
About right (typical)
Signs it is wrong
rows: About the same as the tungsten diameter (1.5–2.5 mm)
Too long: wide, wandering arc, poor control, wider weld, poorer gas cover. Too short: the tungsten touches the pool or the rod.
Tilted about **10–20° from upright**, with the tungsten pointing the way you travel (pushing)
Too steep a tilt pulls air into the gas stream and spreads the heat
About **15–20°** to the plate, low and in line with the joint
Held steeply, the rod melts in the arc instead of the pool and can touch the tungsten
Dabbed into the **front (leading) edge** of the pool
Rod added to the back of the pool or into the arc gives poor fusion and drops of metal
Kept **inside the gas shield**, close to the pool, between dabs
A rod end lifted out of the gas oxidises and carries oxide into the next dab

flow: Hold the torch still and let a small, shiny pool form across both edges of the joint
Dab the rod into the front edge of the pool, then draw it back a little, keeping its end in the gas
Move the torch forward a short distance as the pool settles
Dab again, keeping an even rhythm so the ripples are evenly spaced
Watch the width of the pool: it should stay the same all along the weld

blocks.p: Never just lift the torch away at full current: the crater cools fast and can crack. **Ease off the pedal** (or use the down-slope or crater-fill setting), adding a last dab of rod to fill the crater, then hold the torch still over the end while the **post-flow** covers the weld and the tungsten.

blocks.h: Butt weld in thin sheet, flat (1G)

flow: Clean the edges, fit them tight with no gap, and tack at short distances
Set DCEN, a pointed tungsten, the argon flow and the current from the procedure; test on scrap
Start on a tack at one end; form a pool that melts both edges evenly
Hold the torch 10–20° from upright, pushing, with a short arc
Dab the rod into the front of the pool and move forward in a steady rhythm
Watch the pool sink a little as it penetrates; aim for an even bead on the back
Fill the crater and hold the post-flow at the end

blocks.p: The top edge of a lap heats up and melts away very quickly. Point the arc more at the **bottom sheet**, and let the pool spread across to the top edge. Add the rod at the **top edge** side of the pool, so the edge is filled and not melted back.

flow: Clean both plates, wipe with solvent, and tack the upright square at each end
Set DCEN, the current and gas; test on scrap
If the tungsten cannot reach the root, increase the stick-out a little, using a gas lens so the gas still covers it
Point the torch at about **45° between the plates**, into the root, leaning about 10–20° in the direction of travel
Form a pool that melts into both plates and the root equally
Add the rod at the front of the pool, **towards the upper (upright) plate**, so the weld does not sag onto the bottom plate and leave undercut on the upright
Move steadily so both legs stay equal; fill the crater at the end
When cool, check the legs with a fillet gauge

blocks.p: With the plates upright and the joint running across, gravity pulls the pool down onto the lower plate. Angle the torch slightly **upwards** (about 5–15°), keep the arc short, and add the rod at the **upper edge** of the pool, so the upper toe is filled and does not undercut. Keep the pool small.

blocks.h: Carbon steel, stainless steel and aluminium

head: Point
Carbon steel
Stainless steel
Aluminium
rows: Grind or brush to bright metal; wipe
Its own stainless brush; solvent wipe
Its own stainless brush just before welding; solvent wipe
Porosity from dirt or mill scale
Distortion; heat tint; sugaring on the back without a purge
Aluminium does not glow red before it melts: watch for a shiny, wet pool to form, then add rod quickly. It carries heat away fast, so it needs more current than steel of the same thickness.

blocks.p: On aluminium with AC, a **frosted, white band** forms along each side of the weld. This is the **cleaning action** of the electrode-positive half of the AC cycle stripping off the oxide, and it is normal.

head: Colour on and beside the weld
What it shows
rows: Silver to light straw or gold
Good gas cover and low oxidation
More oxidation: gas cover or heat control could be better
Heavy oxidation: poor gas cover or overheating; the metal will corrode

sections.title: Weld faults, inspection and shutting down

head: Fault
What it looks like
Main causes
How to prevent it
rows: A piece of tungsten trapped in the weld; on an X-ray it shows as a bright spot
Tungsten dipped into the pool or touched by the rod
Current too high for the tungsten size
Short, steady arc with the tungsten clear of the pool and rod
Small flat on the tip; re-point a dirty tungsten
Too little gas, a leak, an empty cylinder, a draught
Set the flow; screen the work; leak-test
A groove melted along the toe and left unfilled
Too little filler at the edges
Add rod at the toe that is undercutting
A small crack, often star-shaped, in the crater at the end
Slope down or ease off the pedal; add a last dab of rod
Weld metal lying on the edges without melting into them
Rod added before a pool has formed, so it melts in the arc
Wait for a pool across both edges
Dab into the pool, not into the arc
Lower current or ease the pedal
Oxidised, sooty or heavily tinted weld
Dark, crusty or rainbow-coloured surface; sugaring on the back of stainless

head: Check
A good TIG weld
rows: Even width and height, with fine, evenly spaced ripples
Fused at both edges, blending smoothly into the metal, with no undercut or overlap
An even line of penetration along the whole length, with no holes or excessive sag
No porosity, cracks or tungsten; little or no oxidation
Both legs equal and at least the size on the drawing, checked with a fillet gauge
Start fused; crater filled with no crack

blocks.p: Write the results on the inspection sheet for each weld (leg size, ripples, undercut, porosity, fusion), mark faults with chalk, and show anything outside the drawing to your instructor.

ul: Mains cable and plug undamaged; test tag in date where the Centre uses them.
Torch cable, work lead and clamp free of cuts, burns and loose connections; work clamp on clean metal.
Cup not cracked or chipped; collet, collet body and back cap the right size and tight.
Tungsten clean, the right type and correctly pointed.
Argon cylinder chained; hose sound; joints leak-tested.
Foot pedal or torch switch working; current, polarity, pre-flow and post-flow set for the job.

flow: Finish the weld, fill the crater and hold the post-flow
Close the argon cylinder valve
Bleed the gas from the hose with the torch switch or gas test button until the flowmeter reads zero
Switch off the machine
Let the torch and tungsten cool, then coil the cables in loose loops off the floor
Put tungstens and filler rods back in their boxes and labelled tubes
Mark hot work, clean the bench, sweep up and report any faults

head: What to report
Examples
What to do
rows: Cracked cup, damaged torch cable, leaking gas fitting, pedal that sticks, HF that will not start the arc
Tag it out of use and tell your instructor
Arc eye, a UV burn on the neck, a tingle from the torch, dizziness in a low space
First aid if needed; report and record it
Unlabelled rods, mixed tungstens, a cylinder with the wrong label, argon running low
Report so they are sorted, replaced or reordered
Welds outside the drawing, faults you could not correct
Record on the inspection sheet and tell your instructor

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain how TIG welding works and what GTAW and TIG stand for.
I can name the hazards of TIG welding, including UV, HF starting, ozone, argon, thoriated dust and solvents, and say how to control each one.
I can choose and check my PPE for TIG welding.
I can choose DCEN or AC for carbon steel, stainless steel and aluminium, and explain why.
I can name the parts of the TIG torch and say what each one does.
I can choose a tungsten type and size, and read its colour band.
I can grind a tungsten correctly and fit it with the matching collet and the right stick-out.
I can set up the argon, set the flow, pre-flow and post-flow, and read the tungsten's colour after welding.
I can clean the work, choose the right filler rod, and fit up and tack thin sheet.
I can hold a short arc and the right torch and rod angles, and dab the rod into the front of the pool.
I can make butt, lap and tee fillet welds in the flat and horizontal positions, and fill the crater.
I can name TIG faults, their causes and how to prevent them.
I can inspect my welds front and back and with a fillet gauge, and record the results.
I can check the TIG set before use, shut it down safely and report faults.

c1.title: Stainless tables in Bog Walk
c1.text: Tanisha is TIG welding 1.5 mm grade 304 stainless steel tables for a food processing plant in Bog Walk, St Catherine. Some ER70S-2 steel rods have been mixed in with her rods. She has been cleaning the joints with the wire brush that hangs by the grinder for general use. The finished welds on her first table range from light straw to dark blue and grey, and the long table top has buckled.

c2.title: Practice butt welds in Morant Bay
c2.text: At a training centre in Morant Bay, St Thomas, Jodi-Ann is TIG welding 2 mm carbon steel sheet in the flat position at about 95 A. She has borrowed a 1.0 mm tungsten. After each weld its tip has melted into a ball and turned dark blue, and she lifts the torch away the moment the arc stops. Between dabs she lifts the filler rod well clear of the cup to see the pool, and its end turns black.

c3.title: Aluminium truck boxes in Linstead
c3.text: Chevaughn is TIG welding 3 mm aluminium sheet into tool boxes for pickup trucks at a shop in Linstead, St Catherine, on an AC machine with pure argon. He notices a frosted white band along each side of his welds. His supervisor tells him he must also choose a filler rod and learn when to add it, because the aluminium never glows before it melts.

c4.title: Brackets in Brown's Town
c4.text: Rojay is TIG welding tee joint brackets in 3 mm carbon steel plate in the horizontal position (2F) at a shop in Brown's Town, St Ann. The drawing asks for 5 mm fillet welds. With the standard collet body and 4 mm of stick-out he cannot get the tungsten into the root. His first welds have undercut on the upright plate, with the weld sagging onto the base plate.

c5.title: A new TIG station in Port Maria
c5.text: Kerine is setting up a new TIG station at a workshop in Port Maria, St Mary, to weld carbon steel. The machine has a positive and a negative socket. The office computer and the shop's card machine sit on a desk two metres from the welding bench. In the drawer she finds tungstens with green, red and gold bands.

questions.q: Why must Tanisha not use the ER70S-2 rods on the stainless tables?
o: The weld metal would not be stainless and would rust
They melt at a far higher heat than stainless steel does
They are coated with flux that spoils the argon shield
They are made only for use with AC on stainless steel
questions.why: A carbon steel rod gives a carbon steel weld in a stainless job: it will rust and may crack. 304 stainless takes 308L rod; rods are kept in labelled tubes so they cannot be mixed up.

questions.q: Rust spots appear beside the welds a few days later. What most likely caused them?
o: The argon flow was set slightly too high for the job
The 308L filler always rusts in salty Jamaican air
Steel particles left by the general-use wire brush
The tables were wiped with acetone before welding
questions.why: A brush used on mild steel leaves tiny steel particles on the stainless surface, and they rust. Stainless steel is cleaned only with a stainless brush kept for it.

questions.q: Which of Tanisha's welds shows the best gas cover?
o: The dark blue welds
The grey welds
They all show the same cover
The light straw welds
questions.why: On stainless steel, silver to light straw shows little oxidation and good gas cover. Darker colours, blue and then grey, show more and more oxidation.

questions.q: How should Tanisha stop the next table top from buckling?
o: Weld each seam in one long run at a higher current
Tack closely, clamp it down and keep the heat low
Leave out the tacks so the sheet can move freely
Cool each weld with water as soon as it is made
questions.why: Stainless steel expands more than mild steel and holds its heat in one place, so it buckles easily. Close tacks, clamping, low heat and short, spread-out welds control it; quenching does not.

questions.q: Why did the tip of Jodi-Ann's 1.0 mm tungsten melt into a ball?
o: The tungsten is too small for 95 A
The argon flow was set too high
DCEN always makes the tip melt round
The sheet was cleaned with acetone
questions.why: A 1.0 mm tungsten is good for only about 80 A on DCEN; above that its tip overheats and melts. A 1.6 mm or 2.4 mm tungsten suits this current.

questions.q: What should Jodi-Ann change so the tungsten comes out bright and silver?
o: Grind a longer and much sharper point on the tungsten
Raise the current so that the arc burns the tungsten clean
Hold the torch still over the weld until the post-flow stops
Turn the pre-flow off so that the gas lasts longer after welding
questions.why: A blue tungsten was still hot when air reached it. Holding the torch in place for the full post-flow (lengthened if needed) protects the tungsten and the crater as they cool.

questions.q: Why is the black end on Jodi-Ann's filler rod a problem?
o: It makes the rod too stiff to bend into the joint
It shows the rod is the wrong grade for carbon steel
It is oxide that goes into the weld at the next dab
It means the argon has been set far too high
questions.why: A hot rod end lifted out of the gas shield oxidises, and the next dab carries that oxide into the pool. Keep the hot end inside the gas, and snip off an oxidised end.

questions.q: What is the frosted white band along Chevaughn's welds?
o: Porosity from too little gas
Burnt filler rod from overheating
Flux residue that must be scrubbed off
The AC cleaning action removing oxide
questions.why: During the electrode-positive half of each AC cycle the arc strips the oxide skin from the aluminium beside the weld, leaving a frosted band. It is normal and shows the cleaning action is working.

questions.q: Which filler rod should Chevaughn use on the aluminium boxes?
o: ER70S-2, as it is the usual TIG filler rod
308L, because it resists corrosion in salt air
Any rod at all, as aluminium needs none
4043 or 5356, as the procedure says
questions.why: Aluminium is welded with an aluminium filler such as 4043 or 5356. Steel and stainless rods will not mix with aluminium, and most joints need filler.

questions.q: Since the aluminium never glows, how does Chevaughn know when to add rod?
o: Wait until the sheet turns a dull red, then dab quickly
When a shiny, wet pool forms under the arc
After a set count of ten seconds at full current
When white smoke starts to rise from the joint
questions.why: Aluminium gives no colour warning before it melts. Watch for the surface to turn into a shiny, wet pool, then add rod at once; aluminium also carries heat away fast.

questions.q: How should Rojay reach the root while keeping good gas cover?
o: Fit a gas lens and set a little more stick-out
Keep the collet body and set 15 mm of stick-out
Remove the cup so the tungsten can get in closer
Hold a much longer arc so it reaches the root
questions.why: A gas lens gives a smooth, even gas flow, so the tungsten can stick out further (often about 10 mm) and still be covered. Long stick-out with a standard collet body, or no cup, leaves the tungsten unshielded.

questions.q: To stop the undercut and sag, where should Rojay add the filler rod?
o: At the back of the pool, on the weld already made
Into the arc, well above the pool, so that it drips in
At the front of the pool, towards the upright plate
At the front of the pool, towards the base plate
questions.why: Gravity pulls the pool down onto the base plate, leaving a groove on the upright. Feeding the rod at the front of the pool on the upper side fills that toe and keeps the legs equal.

questions.q: On one bracket, the fillet gauge shows a 6 mm leg on the base and a 4 mm leg on the upright. Is it acceptable?
o: Yes: the two legs average 5 mm
Yes: the base leg is over size
No: one leg is under size
No: the legs must both be 6 mm
questions.why: Each leg must be at least the size on the drawing; averaging does not count. A 4 mm leg on a 5 mm fillet is under size, and unequal legs show the weld sagged.

questions.q: Which socket does the torch go to for welding carbon steel on DCEN?
o: The positive socket, with the work lead on negative
The negative socket, with the work lead on positive
Either socket, as polarity does not matter for TIG
The positive socket, with no work lead fitted
questions.why: DCEN means the electrode is negative: the torch goes to − and the work lead to +. Most of the heat then goes into the work and the tungsten keeps its point.

questions.q: Why should the computer and the card machine be moved away from the TIG bench?
o: The arc's heat can melt their plastic cases
The argon can leak into their cooling fans
The UV light wipes the data on their chips
The HF start can upset nearby electronics
questions.why: High-frequency arc starting sends out electrical interference that can upset computers, phones and other electronics nearby. Keep them away and follow the maker's instructions.

questions.q: Kerine wants one tungsten that works on DC for steel and on AC for aluminium. Which band should she choose?
o: Gold: lanthanated
Green: pure tungsten
Red: 2% thoriated
None: no such tungsten exists
questions.why: Lanthanated tungsten (gold band for 1.5%) works well on both DC and AC and is not radioactive. Pure tungsten suits AC only; thoriated is mainly for DC and gives radioactive grinding dust.

questions.q: Which filler rod diameter suits TIG welding 1.5 mm carbon steel sheet?
o: About 0.8 mm
About 1.6 mm
About 3.2 mm
About 4.0 mm
questions.why: For thin sheet, a rod about the same diameter as the metal thickness feeds well and melts at the right rate. A 3.2 mm or 4.0 mm rod would chill the small pool.

questions.q: When making a horizontal butt weld (2G), where is the filler rod usually added?
o: At the lower edge of the pool, where the metal sags
At the upper edge of the pool, to fill the top toe
At the back of the pool, after it has frozen
Straight onto the tungsten, so it melts first
questions.why: In 2G the pool sags towards the lower plate, so the upper toe tends to undercut. The torch is angled slightly upwards and the rod is added at the upper edge to fill it.

questions.q: Fabian holds a long TIG arc so that he can see the pool better. What will happen?
o: A narrower, deeper weld with better gas cover
No change, as arc length does not matter in TIG
The tungsten will melt into the weld as filler
A wide, wandering arc with poorer gas cover
questions.why: A long arc spreads and wanders, giving less control, a wider weld and poorer shielding. Keep the arc about as long as the tungsten diameter.

questions.q: Why is a very small flat left on the tip of a pointed tungsten?
o: So the tip does not burn off or break into the weld
So the arc spreads into a wider and flatter weld bead
So the collet can grip the tungsten more tightly
So the tungsten can be used for scratch starting
questions.why: A needle-sharp tip overheats and can break off, leaving a tungsten inclusion. A tiny flat keeps the point strong while the taper still gives a steady arc.
